vignette: The call comes through at 2:14 a.m. for a reported assault at a downtown apartment complex. Elias is twenty-nine then, wearing a badge and carrying the weight of every previous shift. He remembers the stairwell smell of stale tobacco and damp concrete, the way his partner's radio crackles before cutting out. The door gives way. There is shouting, the glint of metal, the sudden lurch forward. His training takes over, his body moving before his mind catches up. Then a sound like a firecracker in a library, followed by a silence that rings in his ears. A man on the floor. A woman screaming. Elias drops to his knees, fingers finding the pulse point that isn't there. He stays there while the world rushes in-paramedics, supervisors, cameras, the cold tile seeping through his uniform. He leaves the department two years later, though he never says exactly why. He starts driving route forty-two, a silver articulated bus that cuts through the northern corridor of the city. The steering wheel is wider than a patrol car's. The seats are vinyl, not leather. He tells himself it's about the schedule and the quiet hum of the engine. At forty-seven, he has been behind that wheel for eight years. He lives alone in a second-floor apartment that stays exactly as he left it each morning. Today, Elias grips the top of the steering wheel at ten and two, his knuckles pale under his gloves. When the bus lurches over a speed bump on Elm, his breath catches, and for a fraction of a second, the dashboard blurs into that stairwell. He blinks, focuses on the rearview, checks the mirror, checks it again. His eyes do this constantly now, mapping exits, counting faces, cataloging threats that aren't there. He hasn't driven past the precinct in five years. The dispatcher knows not to ask about the downtown sector. Elias tells himself it's just traffic, but his foot stays hovering over the brake, ready to catch something that already happened. Passengers don't know what to make of him. He stops at every green light for exactly three seconds longer than necessary, as if giving himself time to decide whether the intersection is safe. A dropped plastic bottle makes his shoulders lock. He doesn't turn around. He just stares at the driver's partition, breathing through his nose until the sound fades. He used to talk with his route mates, traded jokes about the morning commute. Now he sits in silence, listening to the radio but never letting it fill the cab. The noise would only compete with the static that lives in his head. Evenings are the hardest. He cooks one-pan meals, eats quickly, then sits in the dark with the curtains drawn. Sleep comes in fragments. He wakes at the same time every night, heart hammering, convinced he hears the radio squawk. He checks the lock on his door twice, then a third time, before lying back down with his eyes open. Friends from his driving days text occasionally. He leaves the messages. Explaining why he flinches at sudden noises, why he scans every room, feels heavier than the words would be. He is alone, not by choice, but by the quiet erosion of everything that used to connect him to people. In my office, he sits on the edge of the chair, shoulders hunched slightly forward, hands resting on his knees like he's bracing for a sudden stop. He speaks in a low, measured voice, describing his route, his sleep, the way the city moves around him while he stays stuck in the space between the brakes and the gas. He doesn't mention the badge. He doesn't need to.
